questions.q: An implicit meaning is one that is
o: suggested rather than stated
stated directly
in the title
a spelling error
questions.why: You infer it from clues in the text.

questions.q: When asked to answer 'using your own words', you should
o: rephrase the idea without copying key words
quote the whole sentence
write a summary of the passage
give your opinion
questions.why: Lifting the text's words shows no understanding.

questions.q: What does an 'implicit' meaning question ask for?
o: A word copied from the text
A summary
Your opinion of the writer
What is suggested but not stated directly
questions.why: Support inferences with evidence from the text.

questions.q: Read: 'The ferry, which had run every hour since 1952, was cancelled on Tuesday because its engine had broken down.' Why was the ferry cancelled?
o: Because of bad weather on Tuesday
Because its engine had broken down
Because the ferry was too old to run
Because it only ran once an hour
questions.why: This is an explicit question: the reason is stated directly in the sentence ('because its engine had broken down'). The other options are guesses the sentence does not support.

questions.q: Read: 'Maya checked the clock for the fourth time and smoothed her already-smooth skirt.' What does this suggest about Maya?
o: She is bored by her clothes
She cannot read the clock
She is nervous or anxious as she waits
She is late for school
questions.why: Repeatedly checking the time and smoothing a skirt that is already smooth are restless habits, so the writer implies anxiety without stating it.

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'For forty-one years, Edwin Marsh had climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the Gull Point lighthouse every evening at dusk. Tonight was his last climb. The automatic beacon, installed that spring, would take over at midnight, and the keeper's cottage was already half-filled with boxes. He paused on the sixtieth step, as he always did, not because he was tired but because the small window there gave the best view of the harbour lights. “They'll manage without me,” he said aloud, though there was nobody to hear. At the top, he polished the great lens one final time, more carefully than he needed to.' (a) How long had Edwin worked at the lighthouse? [1] (b) Why was this to be his last climb? [1] (c) Why did Edwin pause on the sixtieth step? [1] (d) What does 'though there was nobody to hear' suggest about Edwin's situation? [2] (e) What does polishing the lens 'more carefully than he needed to' suggest about his feelings? [2]
scheme: B1: (a) forty-one years
B1: (b) an automatic beacon would take over (from midnight)
B1: (c) for the view of the harbour lights (not because he was tired)
B1: (d) he is alone or isolated
B1: (d) he is talking to himself, perhaps to reassure himself that leaving is all right
B1: (e) he is sad or reluctant to leave and wants to make the moment last
B1: (e) he takes pride in his work and cares about doing it properly

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'Ten years ago, keeping bees on a city rooftop would have seemed eccentric. Today, the town of Marlow Vale has over three hundred registered hives, many on the flat roofs of offices and schools. Supporters argue that urban bees actually do better than their country cousins: city gardens and parks offer a wider variety of flowers, and fewer pesticides are used. Not everyone is convinced. Some ecologists warn that too many honeybees may compete with wild bees for a limited supply of pollen, and a few residents have complained about swarms appearing on balconies in early summer.' (a) How many registered hives does Marlow Vale have? [1] (b) Give two reasons why supporters think urban bees do better. [2] (c) Explain the concern raised by some ecologists. [2] (d) Which word in the first sentence shows that rooftop beekeeping once seemed unusual? [1] (e) What problem have some residents reported? [1]
scheme: B1: (a) over three hundred
B1: (b) a wider variety of flowers (in gardens and parks)
B1: (b) fewer pesticides are used
B1: (c) too many honeybees compete with wild bees
B1: (c) for a limited supply of pollen, so wild bees may suffer
B1: (d) 'eccentric'
B1: (e) swarms appearing on balconies (in early summer)

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'When the results were finally read out, the town held its breath. Nobody had expected the tiny team from Brackley to reach the final, least of all their coach, who had spent the season apologising for them. Now, as the scores were confirmed, he allowed himself a reluctant smile, and then – to the delight of the crowd – a most undignified little dance.' (a) Using your own words, explain what the writer means by each of these phrases: (i) 'the town held its breath' (ii) 'least of all their coach' (iii) 'a reluctant smile' (iv) 'a most undignified little dance'. [4] (b) What had the coach done all season, and what does this suggest about his opinion of the team? [2]
scheme: B1: (i) everyone waited in tense, anxious silence
B1: (ii) the coach expected it even less than anyone else
B1: (iii) a smile he tried to hold back or was unwilling to show
B1: (iv) a silly, embarrassing dance that did not suit his serious position
B1: (b) he had kept apologising for the team
B1: (b) he thought they were weak and had low expectations of them

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'Aunt Rosa's kitchen had not changed in twenty years. The same blue tiles, the same chipped cups lined up by size, the same calendar from a bakery that had closed long ago. She greeted me at the door with a kiss on each cheek and a quick glance at my shoes. “You've come by bus,” she said. It was not a question.' (a) Give two details that show the kitchen has not changed. [2] (b) What does 'cups lined up by size' suggest about Aunt Rosa? [1] (c) Why do you think Aunt Rosa glances at the narrator's shoes? [1] (d) Explain what 'It was not a question' suggests about Aunt Rosa. [2]
scheme: B1: (a) one of: the same blue tiles / the same chipped cups
B1: (a) a second detail, e.g. a calendar from a bakery that closed long ago
B1: (b) she is orderly, precise or particular
B1: (c) to check whether they are dirty or muddy, showing she notices everything (and can tell how the narrator travelled)
B1: (d) she is certain and confident in her judgement: a sharp observer
B1: (d) she may be disapproving, so the narrator feels judged

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'The council's plan to close Fenton Road library and move its books into the new shopping centre has divided residents. Councillor Ade Bello says the move will save £80,000 a year and bring the library “to where people actually are”. Opening hours will increase from 30 to 50 hours a week. But regular user Joan Pike, 78, is unhappy. “The shopping centre is two bus rides away for me,” she says. “And where will the children go after school? The old library was quiet. A shopping centre is not.”' (a) How much money will the move save each year? [1] (b) By how many hours a week will opening times increase? [1] (c) What does Councillor Bello mean by bringing the library 'to where people actually are'? [1] (d) Give two reasons why Joan Pike objects. [2] (e) How does the writer present the issue in a balanced way? [1]
scheme: B1: (b) 20 hours (from 30 to 50)
B1: (c) more people visit the shopping centre than the old library, so it will be easier to reach and better used
B1: (d) the shopping centre is two bus rides away for her (harder to reach)
B1: (d) it will not be a quiet place for children to go after school
B1: (e) it quotes both a supporter and an opponent of the plan

questions.q: A good summary
o: selects the relevant points and writes them concisely in your own words
copies sentences in order
adds your opinion
includes every example
questions.why: Selection and concision are what's rewarded.

questions.q: Before writing a summary, you should first
o: identify the points that answer the question
write the conclusion
count words in the passage
find quotations
questions.why: Plan the content, then write it fluently.

questions.q: In a summary, which approach works best?
o: Select the relevant points and write them concisely in your own words
Copy whole sentences
Add examples of your own
Comment on the language
questions.why: Keep to the length set.

questions.q: A summary task asks for the difficulties faced by early settlers. Which sentence from the passage should you leave out?
o: Fresh water had to be carried up from the river each day.
Winters were longer and harsher than anyone had expected.
The settlers named their village after a hill in their homeland.
Crops failed again and again in the thin, stony soil.
questions.why: Naming the village is not a difficulty, so it is irrelevant to the question. The other three are all hardships and belong in the summary.

questions.q: Which is the best summary, in your own words, of: 'The town's buses are often late, frequently overcrowded and, on Sundays, do not run at all'?
o: The town's buses are often late and frequently overcrowded.
The buses, which are frequently late, are often overcrowded and do not run at all on Sundays.
I think the buses are terrible and the council should fix them.
Buses are unreliable, crowded and absent on Sundays.
questions.why: It keeps all three points, is concise and uses fresh words. The others either drop a point, copy the original wording, or add an opinion.

long.q: Summarise, in no more than 120 words, the reasons a writer gives for a change they describe (use a passage of your choice). Use this scheme to mark yourself.
scheme: B1: 8 or more relevant points selected
B1: points written in your own words
B1: concise: no examples, repetition or opinion
B1: organised and fluent, within the word limit

long.q: Read the passage, then summarise the reasons why people in middle age take up running. Write no more than 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Why do so many people in their forties and fifties suddenly take up running? For some, it begins with a health warning: a doctor mentions blood pressure, and a gentle jog seems the cheapest remedy. Others want time alone. “It's the only hour of the day when nobody needs anything from me,” says one mother of three. Running also offers measurable progress at an age when careers can feel stuck; shaving thirty seconds off a personal best brings a real sense of achievement. Many join clubs and find a new circle of friends. And then there is the simple pleasure of being outdoors, noticing the seasons change on the same familiar route. Of course, not everyone sticks with it: knee injuries are common, and dark winter evenings defeat many beginners.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: health concerns, e.g. a doctor's warning about blood pressure
B1: it is a cheap way to get fit
B1: time alone, away from other people's demands
B1: visible progress and achievement when careers may be stuck
B1: making friends through clubs
B1: the enjoyment of being outdoors and seeing the seasons change
B1: own words, concise, within 80 words, and no drawbacks (injuries, winter) included

long.q: Read the passage, then summarise the problems caused by increased tourism on Tavor Island. Write no more than 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'When the ferry service to Tavor Island doubled in 2018, local businesses celebrated. Six years later, the mood is mixed. In summer the island's single road is jammed with hire cars, and the fresh water supply, which comes from one reservoir, has twice run dry in August. House prices have risen so sharply that young islanders, priced out by holiday-home buyers, are moving to the mainland. Fishermen complain that tour boats crowd the harbour, and the island's school has lost a third of its pupils. Visitors do bring money – the café owners are delighted – but many residents feel the island no longer belongs to them.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: traffic congestion on the only road
B1: water shortages (the reservoir has run dry)
B1: rising house prices force young islanders to leave
B1: tour boats crowd the harbour, causing problems for fishermen
B1: the school is losing pupils
B1: residents feel they have lost ownership of their island
B1: own words, within 80 words, and no benefits (money, cafés) included

long.q: A student wrote this summary of a passage about fast fashion: 'The writer says that in my opinion fast fashion is really bad because “clothes are worn only seven times before being thrown away” and also it's bad for workers and also the environment, for example rivers in Bangladesh are polluted with dyes, which is terrible.' Identify four weaknesses in this summary, then rewrite it in no more than 40 words.
scheme: B1: includes personal opinion or comment ('in my opinion', 'which is terrible')
B1: copies a quotation instead of using own words
B1: includes a specific example (the rivers in Bangladesh) that should be generalised or left out
B1: repetitive, loose linking ('and also... and also') rather than concise, fluent sentences
B1: a rewrite in own words within 40 words, e.g. 'Fast fashion is harmful: garments are discarded after very few wears, factory workers are exploited and dyes pollute the environment.'

long.q: Read the passage, then summarise the benefits of sleep described in it. Write no more than 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Scientists now believe that sleep is far more than rest. During deep sleep, the brain sorts and stores what was learned during the day, which is why students who sleep well before an exam often recall more. Sleep also helps regulate mood: teenagers who regularly get fewer than seven hours are more likely to feel anxious or irritable. The body repairs muscle and releases growth hormone at night, and a well-rested immune system fights off colds more effectively. There is even evidence that tired drivers react as slowly as those who have drunk alcohol. Yet many teenagers stay up late scrolling through their phones, whose blue light delays the release of the sleep hormone melatonin.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: memory: the brain stores what was learned, so recall is better
B1: mood: less anxiety and irritability
B1: physical repair and growth (muscle repair, growth hormone)
B1: a stronger immune system that fights off illness
B1: alertness: quicker reactions, e.g. when driving
B1: own words, concise, within 80 words, and nothing about phones or blue light

questions.q: 'The wind howled like a wounded animal' is an example of
o: a simile
a metaphor
alliteration
onomatopoeia only
questions.why: It compares using 'like'.

questions.q: In a language question you earn most credit for
o: explaining the effect of specific word choices
naming as many techniques as possible
retelling the plot
quoting long passages
questions.why: Analysis of effect beats technique-spotting.

questions.q: Connotation means
o: the associations a word carries
the dictionary definition
a word's spelling
the word's origin
questions.why: e.g. 'lair' suggests danger in a way 'home' does not.

questions.q: 'The old house groaned and sighed in the storm.' Which technique is used, and what is its effect?
o: Personification, making the house seem alive and suffering
A simile, comparing the house to a person
Alliteration, creating a gentle, soothing rhythm
Onomatopoeia, copying the exact sound of the wind
questions.why: Groaning and sighing are human actions given to a house, which is personification; it makes the house seem to suffer and adds an uneasy atmosphere. There is no 'like' or 'as', so it is not a simile.

questions.q: A student writes about 'The classroom was a furnace'. Which comment earns the most credit?
o: This is a metaphor.
The metaphor 'furnace' exaggerates the heat, suggesting it is suffocating and almost unbearable for the students.
This is a simile because it compares the classroom to something.
The writer uses good vocabulary here to make it interesting.
questions.why: Credit comes from explaining the effect of a precise word. Naming the technique alone earns little, 'simile' is wrong, and 'good vocabulary' is too vague.

long.q: Re-read a paragraph of description from a passage you are studying. Choose three words or phrases and explain how each creates an effect. (Practise on any unseen passage; mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: three well-chosen, precise words or phrases (not whole sentences)
B1: the meaning of each explained in context
B1: the effect on the reader explained (what it makes you feel or picture)
B1: links between choices, e.g. a pattern of violent or calm imagery

long.q: Read the passage. 'The storm arrived without courtesy. It shouldered its way down the valley, ripping slates from roofs and flinging them into the lanes like playing cards. The river, usually a lazy brown ribbon, swelled and snarled, gnawing at its banks. By midnight the whole village was cowering behind shutters, listening to the wind's long, furious howl.' Explain how the writer uses language to convey the power of the storm.
scheme: B1: 'without courtesy' and 'shouldered its way' personify the storm as a rude, forceful bully that pushes through unstopped
B1: the simile 'like playing cards' makes heavy slates seem light and flimsy, emphasising the storm's strength
B1: the contrast between 'lazy brown ribbon' and 'swelled and snarled, gnawing' turns the gentle river into a fierce animal
B1: 'cowering' shows the villagers' fear and helplessness
B1: the sound image 'long, furious howl' suggests a wild, wolf-like threat
B1: links between choices explained, e.g. a pattern of violent, animal imagery that builds a sense of menace

long.q: Read the passage. 'At eight o'clock the station swallowed the city whole. Commuters poured down the escalators in a grey, unbroken river, their faces fixed on phones, their coffee cups held aloft like small trophies. Announcements crackled overhead and nobody listened. Somewhere a child was crying, a thin, bright sound that cut through the shuffle of a thousand shoes.' Choose three words or phrases and explain how each helps to create the atmosphere of the station.
scheme: B1: a precise first choice, e.g. 'swallowed the city whole'
B1: its effect explained, e.g. the station is a huge monster consuming everyone: overwhelming scale
B1: a precise second choice, e.g. 'grey, unbroken river' or 'coffee cups held aloft like small trophies'
B1: its effect explained, e.g. a dull, anonymous, relentless mass of people / small daily rituals made to look comically important
B1: a precise third choice, e.g. 'nobody listened' or 'a thin, bright sound that cut through'
B1: its effect explained, e.g. indifference and noise / one small, vulnerable voice standing out against the monotony

long.q: Read the passage. 'Mrs Okafor ran the corner shop the way a general runs a campaign. Every tin faced forward; every price was written in her sharp, upright capitals. Children who entered with sticky fingers were stopped at the door by a single raised eyebrow. Yet when old Mr Davies forgot his purse, she waved him away with a gruff “Pay me Tuesday,” and slipped an extra loaf into his bag.' Explain how the writer's language presents Mrs Okafor as a more complex character than she first seems.
scheme: B1: the simile 'the way a general runs a campaign' presents her as disciplined, commanding and in control
B1: 'Every tin faced forward' and 'sharp, upright capitals' continue the military image: strict order and precision
B1: 'a single raised eyebrow' shows authority without a word: intimidating to children
B1: 'Yet' marks a turn, revealing a hidden kindness that contrasts with her stern image
B1: 'gruff' and 'slipped an extra loaf' show her generosity is quiet and disguised behind a rough manner

long.q: Read the two paragraphs. 'The lake lay still under the morning mist, silver and silent, and the only movement was a heron lifting itself lazily from the reeds.' 'Then the engine roared. A jet-ski tore across the water, slicing the silver into ragged white strips, and the heron vanished with a startled shriek.' Explain how the writer uses language to create a contrast between the two paragraphs.
scheme: B1: sibilance in 'still... silver and silent' creates a hushed, peaceful mood
B1: 'lifting itself lazily' suggests slow, gentle movement and calm
B1: the short sentence 'Then the engine roared.' makes an abrupt shift to sudden noise
B1: violent verbs 'tore' and 'slicing', and 'ragged', suggest the destruction of beauty
B1: the 'silver' of the first paragraph is literally cut up: the calm image is broken
B1: 'lazily' becomes 'vanished with a startled shriek': nature's peace is shattered by human intrusion

questions.q: In an extended response (e.g. a letter or speech based on a text), you should
o: use and develop ideas from the text in the required form
copy the text's structure
ignore the text
write a story
questions.why: Reading marks come from using the text's ideas, writing marks from form and audience.

questions.q: In the extended response to reading, what matters?
o: Using and developing ideas from the text in the form asked
Ignoring the text
Copying long extracts
Writing a story
questions.why: Write in the voice and form the task gives.

questions.q: What tone should an extended response written as a character have?
o: Your own normal voice
One that fits the character and situation in the text
A formal report
Slang throughout
questions.why: Use details from the text to make the voice convincing.

questions.q: You are asked to write a journal entry as a character from the passage. Which approach scores highest for reading?
o: Retell the events in exactly the same order as the passage
Invent exciting new events that the passage does not mention
Develop the character's thoughts about the events, inferring feelings the passage only hints at
Analyse the writer's use of language techniques
questions.why: High reading marks come from using and developing the passage's ideas, including inferences, in the character's voice. Retelling is limited, invention moves away from the text, and analysis is the wrong task.

questions.q: In the extended response, how should you use details from the passage?
o: Select relevant details and adapt them to the new form and voice
Copy long phrases word for word to prove you read it
Avoid them completely so your writing is original
Use details from the first paragraph only
questions.why: The task rewards selecting and reworking ideas from across the passage to suit the new form. Copying is penalised, and ignoring the text loses reading marks.

long.q: Read the passage. 'Plans for a skate park in Willow Gardens have sparked fierce debate. The council says the park will give the town's 4,000 teenagers somewhere safe to go, and that youth groups have asked for one for years. A local skater, 15-year-old Theo, says skaters are currently moved on from the shopping-centre car park “almost every night”. But neighbours fear noise late into the evening, litter, and the loss of a quiet lawn used by older residents and young families. The council has promised to close the park at 9 p.m. and to plant a hedge to reduce noise.' You live near Willow Gardens. Write a letter to your local newspaper giving your views on the plan (250–350 words), using ideas from the passage. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: at least three relevant ideas from the passage used
B1: ideas developed with your own inferences (e.g. what being moved on 'every night' says about teenagers' lives) rather than copied
B1: a clear viewpoint that deals with both the benefits and the neighbours' worries, including the council's promises
B1: letter conventions and a register suited to newspaper readers
B1: well-organised paragraphs with clear links
B1: accurate, fluent expression

long.q: Read the passage. 'Every night in nesting season, volunteers patrol Kanu Beach from 9 p.m. until dawn. Their job is to spot female turtles coming ashore, record the location of each nest and protect the eggs from dogs and poachers. When the hatchlings emerge, around fifty days later, volunteers make sure the tiny turtles reach the sea, keeping torches off because bright lights lead them inland. The work is exhausting and unpaid: volunteers sleep in tents, cook on a single stove and are bitten mercilessly by sandflies. Yet most return the following year. “Watching a hatchling hit the water for the first time,” says coordinator Lena Ruiz, “you forget every bite.”' You are a volunteer at Kanu Beach. Write two journal entries (250–350 words in total): one for a night early in the nesting season and one for the night the eggs hatched. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the volunteers' duties covered: patrol hours, recording nests, protecting eggs from dogs and poachers
B1: the hatching covered, with understanding of why torches are kept off
B1: hardships (tents, one stove, sandflies) used, and feelings inferred: exhaustion, frustration, pride, wonder
B1: plausible development beyond the passage in your own words, not copied phrases
B1: a convincing journal voice: first person, personal, reflective, dated entries
B1: organised and accurate

long.q: Read the passage. 'From September, Hillcrest Academy will require students to lock their phones in pouches during the school day. The head teacher, Mr Sato, points to a survey in which 60% of teachers said phones disrupted lessons weekly, and to cases of online bullying that began in the playground. Some parents welcome the ban; others worry they will not be able to contact their children in an emergency. Students are divided: many admit they check their phones too often, but they also use them for timetables, music practice apps and, for some, as calculators.' You are a student at Hillcrest. Write a speech to your year group giving your views on the ban (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: arguments for the ban used: disrupted lessons (the 60% survey), online bullying, students' overuse
B1: arguments against used: emergency contact, timetables, practice apps, calculators
B1: these points evaluated to reach a clear view, possibly a reasoned compromise
B1: speech conventions: addresses the year group directly, uses rhetorical techniques
B1: ideas expressed in your own words, not copied from the passage
B1: organised and accurate

long.q: Read the passage. 'At 92, Hilda Brennan still remembers the night the Regent Cinema opened in 1949. “There was a red carpet, and the manager wore white gloves,” she laughs. She went on to work there as an usher for thirty years, selling ice creams in the interval and once helping to calm a crowd when a reel of film caught fire. The Regent closed in 1988 and has stood empty since, but a community group has now raised £200,000 to reopen it as an arts centre. Hilda has been invited to cut the ribbon.' Write the words of an interview between a local radio presenter and Hilda (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: interview form: the presenter's questions and Hilda's answers clearly set out
B1: details of the opening night and her work used (red carpet, white gloves, thirty years as an usher, ice creams, the fire)
B1: the cinema's later history used (closed in 1988, £200,000 raised, the ribbon-cutting)
B1: Hilda's feelings inferred and developed: nostalgia, pride, excitement
B1: distinct voices: the presenter's prompting questions and Hilda's personal, lively speech
B1: accurate and fluent

long.q: Read the passage. 'The Year 10 trip to the Coastal Science Centre had been planned for months, but little went to plan. The coach arrived forty minutes late, so the morning rock-pool session was cut short. Rain then forced the afternoon fieldwork indoors, where the centre's lab could only hold half the group at a time. Even so, students praised the marine biologist, Dr Kim, whose talk on plastic pollution was “the best part of the day”. Several suggested that next year the trip should run in June rather than March, and that the school should use a different coach company.' As student representative, write a report for your head teacher evaluating the trip and making recommendations (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: report conventions: title, to/from, headings, formal register
B1: problems identified accurately: late coach, shortened rock-pool session, rain, the lab holding only half the group
B1: the positive identified: Dr Kim's talk on plastic pollution
B1: recommendations: June instead of March, a different coach company, plus a sensible idea of your own (e.g. a planned rotation for the lab)
B1: an overall judgement on whether the trip was worthwhile, inferred from the evidence
B1: clear and accurate

questions.q: Directed writing tests your ability to
o: evaluate ideas from texts and write for a purpose and audience
write a story
describe a picture
correct grammar
questions.why: You must select, evaluate and argue from the source material.

questions.q: A discursive piece should
o: consider different viewpoints before reaching a view
argue only one side
be informal
avoid paragraphs
questions.why: Balance is the key feature.

questions.q: In directed writing, what gains marks for reading?
o: Listing the ideas
Writing your own unrelated views
Quoting at length
Evaluating and developing the ideas from the texts
questions.why: Writing marks reward audience, structure and accuracy.

questions.q: Which opening is most suitable for a letter to the editor of a local newspaper?
o: Hey there, editor! Guess what I think about the library?
Library closing = bad idea!!!
To whom it may concern, lol this is about the library.
Dear Editor, I am writing in response to your recent article on the plan to close the town library.
questions.why: A letter to an editor needs a formal register and a clear statement of purpose. The others are too informal, use text-speak or overuse exclamation marks.

questions.q: Two texts disagree about building a new road. What does it mean to 'evaluate' them in directed writing?
o: Judge how convincing each argument is and explain why
Copy the main points of each text in order
Count how many arguments each text makes
Summarise only the text you agree with
questions.why: Evaluation means weighing the ideas, for example noticing an argument is based on opinion rather than evidence. Listing or copying points is only summary.

long.q: Write a speech to your school's parents arguing whether homework should be banned for students under 16. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a clear view, developed and sustained
B1: counter-arguments considered and answered
B1: register suited to the audience (parents) and the form (a speech)
B1: well-structured paragraphs with linking
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Read the two texts. Text A: 'Modern zoos are arks. Breeding programmes have saved species such as the Arabian oryx from extinction, and the money visitors spend funds field research. Children who see a living tiger are more likely to care about protecting wild ones.' Text B: 'However spacious the enclosure, a zoo is still a cage. Elephants that roam many kilometres a day in the wild pace the same few metres in captivity, and many show signs of stress. Only a small fraction of zoo species are endangered, so conservation is often an excuse for entertainment.' Write an article for your school magazine evaluating both views and giving your own (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: Text A's ideas used and evaluated: breeding programmes, funding research, inspiring children
B1: Text B's ideas used and evaluated: confinement, stress, few endangered species
B1: the strength of each argument judged (e.g. one success story against a general claim; whether stress can be reduced)
B1: a clear, consistent view of your own
B1: article form and register suited to students: title, engaging opening, direct address
B1: well-structured and accurate

long.q: Read the two texts. Text A (a developer's leaflet): '250 new homes, 30% of them affordable, a new primary school and a bus service to town. Young families who grew up in Oakley can finally afford to stay.' Text B (a resident's blog): 'The fields at Oakley Farm flood every winter, and the single-lane road already backs up at school time. Our doctor's surgery has a three-week wait. Where will 250 more families go when they are ill?' Write a letter to the local council giving your views on the plan (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the benefits used and evaluated: affordable homes, the school, the bus service, local families staying
B1: the concerns used and evaluated: flooding, traffic, the surgery's waiting time
B1: claims questioned or inferences drawn, e.g. whether 30% affordable is enough, who builds on a flood plain, what the developer gains
B1: a clear viewpoint with letter conventions and a formal register
B1: well-organised and persuasive
B1: accurate expression

long.q: Read the two texts. Text A (a teacher): 'Exams test what students can do on their own, under the same conditions for everyone. They are fair precisely because they are harsh.' Text B (a student): 'One bad morning shouldn't decide two years of work. Coursework lets us show research, creativity and the ability to improve – the skills employers actually ask for.' Write a speech to the students in your year group arguing whether coursework should replace exams (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: ideas from both texts used
B1: the ideas evaluated, e.g. fairness against real skills, and inferences such as the risk of help at home with coursework
B1: a clear, sustained view
B1: speech features: direct address, rhetorical questions, a register suited to fellow students
B1: organised and accurate

long.q: Read the two texts. Text A (the youth club leader's notes): 'We have £5,000 to spend. Option 1: a games room with table tennis and consoles, used every week, all year, by all 80 members. Option 2: a five-day exchange with a youth club in Lyon for 20 members.' Text B (an email from a member): 'The Lyon trip would be the experience of a lifetime – most of us have never been abroad. A games room just keeps us indoors staring at screens.' Write a report for the club committee assessing both options and making a recommendation (250–350 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: report format: title, purpose, sections, formal register
B1: the games room evaluated: year-round use by all 80 members, good value per member
B1: the trip evaluated: a rare experience, but for only 20 of the 80 members
B1: further issues inferred, e.g. how the 20 are chosen, running costs, and that table tennis is not a screen activity
B1: a reasoned recommendation that follows from the assessment
B1: clear and accurate

questions.q: The best descriptive writing usually
o: focuses on sensory detail and atmosphere rather than plot
tells a long story
uses lists of adjectives
is written in the second person
questions.why: Description creates a scene, not a sequence of events.

questions.q: What makes descriptive writing effective?
o: A fast-moving plot
Precise detail and imagery that build an atmosphere
Lots of dialogue
A list of events
questions.why: Description focuses on senses and impressions, not events.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest description?
o: It was cold and nobody was there.
The park was very, very cold.
Frost silvered the empty benches, and our breath hung in the still air.
I went to the park and then went home.
questions.why: Precise verbs and sensory detail create atmosphere.

questions.q: Why might a writer use a single, very short sentence as its own paragraph in a description?
o: To list every object in the scene
Because the description has run out of detail
To create emphasis or a sudden shift in mood at a key moment
To change from past to present tense
questions.why: A short, isolated sentence stands out after longer ones, so it can emphasise a detail or mark a change in atmosphere.

questions.q: Which sentence makes the best use of senses other than sight?
o: The kitchen was big and bright.
The kitchen had a table and four chairs.
The kitchen was nice and clean.
Onions hissed in the pan and the sharp smell of lemon filled the kitchen.
questions.why: It appeals to sound ('hissed') and smell ('sharp smell of lemon'), building atmosphere. The others are plain visual statements with vague adjectives.

long.q: Describe a market at the moment it opens in the morning. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a vivid, sustained atmosphere rather than a story
B1: precise sensory detail (sounds, smells, light)
B1: varied sentence structures for effect
B1: ambitious, well-chosen vocabulary
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Describe an airport departure lounge late at night. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a sustained atmosphere (tiredness, waiting, stillness) rather than a story
B1: precise sensory detail: flickering screens, announcements, the hum of floor cleaners
B1: focus moving between the wide scene and individual people
B1: varied sentence structures and well-chosen vocabulary
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Describe a place you know well, first on a summer afternoon and then on a winter morning. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a clear, deliberate contrast between the two seasons
B1: precise sensory detail in both parts (light, temperature, sound, colour)
B1: a controlled two-part structure, perhaps with echoing images
B1: ambitious, well-chosen vocabulary and imagery
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Describe a crowd waiting for a famous person to arrive. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a building sense of anticipation, without the description becoming a narrative
B1: zooms in from the whole crowd to a few individuals and details
B1: sound and movement used to show the crowd's mood
B1: varied sentences used for effect, e.g. short sentences as tension peaks
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Describe an abandoned fairground. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: an atmosphere of emptiness and decay sustained throughout
B1: original imagery (personification, metaphor) rather than clichés
B1: a deliberate structure, e.g. moving through the space or contrasting past and present
B1: a range of sentence forms and precise vocabulary
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

questions.q: A strong narrative usually has
o: a clear structure with a developed climax and resolution
as many characters as possible
no dialogue
a dream ending
questions.why: Control of structure is what's rewarded.

questions.q: What helps a narrative most?
o: Many characters
A clear structure with a developed ending
Long descriptions with no events
An unfinished ending
questions.why: Control pace and choose a focused plot.

questions.q: Why plan a narrative before writing?
o: To use more time
Plans earn marks on their own
To make it longer
So the plot is controlled and the ending is reached
questions.why: A short, well-shaped story beats a long, unfinished one.

questions.q: Which opening is most likely to hook a reader?
o: Once upon a time there was a girl called Sara.
This is a story about my holiday last summer.
The letter had been lying under the door for three days before anyone dared to open it.
I woke up, had breakfast and went to school.
questions.why: It creates mystery and tension straight away, making the reader ask why no one opened the letter. The others are predictable or simply list events.

questions.q: Why might a writer choose a first-person narrator for a story?
o: To show what every character is thinking at once
To let the reader share one character's thoughts and feelings closely
To avoid having to use any dialogue
To make the story longer
questions.why: A first-person narrator ('I') gives direct access to one character's mind, which builds closeness. Showing every character's thoughts is what an omniscient third-person narrator does.

long.q: Write a story called 'The Locked Door'. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: an engaging opening
B1: a clear plot with tension and a convincing resolution
B1: believable characters developed through action and dialogue
B1: a setting that supports the mood
B1: varied sentences and paragraphs to control pace
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, including dialogue punctuation

long.q: Write a story that begins: 'Nobody noticed when the lights went out at first.' Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: the given opening used naturally and developed with intrigue
B1: a well-paced plot that builds to a climax
B1: characters whose reactions are believable
B1: an ending that is satisfying or deliberately unsettling
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Write a story in which a misunderstanding has serious consequences. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: the misunderstanding set up clearly and credibly
B1: consequences that grow logically and raise the tension
B1: characters' motives and feelings shown through action and dialogue
B1: a resolution that ties the plot together
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Write a story that ends with the words: '...and that was the last time I trusted a map.' Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: the ending prepared for, so the final line feels earned
B1: a clear journey or adventure with rising tension
B1: a distinctive first-person voice, perhaps with humour
B1: vivid setting and pacing that varies between action and reflection
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Write a story called 'The Return' about a character coming home after a long absence. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: the absence and its reasons revealed gradually rather than explained all at once
B1: changes in the place and people used to create emotion
B1: a developed main character with an inner life
B1: a structured plot with a meaningful ending
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: It's raining, so we stayed in.
Its raining so, we stayed in.
It's raining so we stayed, in.
Its' raining, so we stayed in.
questions.why: It's = it is; the comma comes before 'so'.

questions.q: A comma splice is
o: two main clauses joined only by a comma
a list with commas
a comma before 'and'
a missing apostrophe
questions.why: Use a full stop, semicolon or conjunction instead.

questions.q: Which is correct?
o: Its raining, so the dog stays in it's kennel.
It's raining, so the dog stays in it's kennel.
Its raining, so the dog stays in its kennel.
It's raining, so the dog stays in its kennel.
questions.why: It's = it is; its shows possession.

questions.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
o: I was tired, I went to bed.
I was tired; I went to bed.
I was tired I went to bed.
I was tired: and I went to bed.
questions.why: A comma cannot join two complete sentences (comma splice).

questions.q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
o: The box of pencils were on the desk.
Each of the players has a locker.
The results of the test was surprising.
Everyone in the room were silent.
questions.why: 'Each' is singular, so it takes 'has'. In the others the verb does not agree with the true subject: 'box' needs 'was', 'results' needs 'were' and 'everyone' needs 'was'.

long.q: Rewrite this sentence with correct punctuation and capital letters: its raining again said maya lets stay inside
scheme: B1: capital letters at the start of each sentence and for 'Maya'
B1: apostrophes in 'It's' and 'Let's'
B1: speech marks around each spoken part
B1: a comma inside the speech marks before 'said', and full stops after 'Maya' and 'inside'
long.ans: "It's raining again," said Maya. "Let's stay inside."

long.q: Correct the five spelling errors in this sentence: 'The goverment recieved alot of complaints about the noisey enviroment.'
scheme: B1: government
B1: received
B1: a lot (two words)
B1: noisy
B1: environment
long.ans: government; received; a lot; noisy; environment

long.q: Each sentence has one error. Rewrite it correctly. (a) I was tired, I went to bed. (b) Walking to school, the rain started. (c) Me and him went to the shop. (d) Each of the students have a locker. (e) The team played good.
scheme: B1: (a) comma splice fixed, e.g. 'I was tired, so I went to bed.' or 'I was tired; I went to bed.'
B1: (b) dangling modifier fixed, e.g. 'As I was walking to school, the rain started.'
B1: (c) 'He and I went to the shop.'
B1: (d) 'Each of the students has a locker.'
B1: (e) 'The team played well.'

long.q: Choose the correct word in each sentence. (a) The new rules will (affect / effect) everyone. (b) (Their / There / They're) coats are on the floor. (c) I'd rather walk (than / then) wait. (d) Be careful or you'll (lose / loose) your keys. (e) The (principal / principle) of the school gave a speech. (f) She gave me some good (advice / advise).
scheme: B1: (a) affect
B1: (b) Their
B1: (c) than
B1: (d) lose
B1: (e) principal
B1: (f) advice
long.ans: affect; Their; than; lose; principal; advice

long.q: Rewrite each sentence, adding the missing punctuation. (a) the childrens toys were everywhere (b) I need three things eggs flour and milk (c) she loved the city however she missed the sea (d) the dogs bowl was empty (there is one dog) (e) the two girls bags were stolen
scheme: B1: (a) The children's toys were everywhere.
B1: (b) I need three things: eggs, flour and milk.
B1: (c) She loved the city; however, she missed the sea.
B1: (d) The dog's bowl was empty.
B1: (e) The two girls' bags were stolen.
